title: Centripetal Acceleration
short: Moving in a circle at steady speed means accelerating toward the center: a = v²/r.
trouble: Students think an object moving at a constant speed can't be accelerating.

blocks.html: Velocity is a vector, so it can change in two ways: in size or in direction. Acceleration and Its Sign includes both. A car rounding a curve at a steady speed is accelerating, because its direction keeps turning.

An object moving at steady speed $v$ around a circle of radius $r$ accelerates toward the center with $\role[centripetal acceleration]{acceleration}{a_c} = \dfrac{\role[speed]{velocity}{v}^2}{\role[radius]{position}{r}}$.

Take the velocity at two nearby moments and subtract them as vectors: the change points toward the center of the circle. How big is it? In time $\Delta t$ the velocity turns through the same angle as the radius, $\Delta\theta = v\Delta t/r$, so the change has size about $v\,\Delta\theta = v^2\Delta t/r$. Divide by $\Delta t$: $a = v^2/r$. Faster means the velocity is both bigger and turning sooner, which is why $v$ is squared.

blocks.name: ph-circular

opts.task: Change the speed and the radius. Doubling v makes the acceleration four times as big.

blocks.cap: Steady speed, changing direction: the velocity is along the path and the acceleration points to the center.

blocks.title: A car on a curve
blocks.q: A car rounds a curve of radius $50\ \text{m}$ at $15\ \text{m/s}$. Find its acceleration.
steps: $a_c = \dfrac{15^2}{50} = \dfrac{225}{50} = 4.5\ \text{m/s}^2$, toward the center of the curve.

blocks.title: From the period
blocks.q: A carousel horse $5\ \text{m}$ from the center goes around once every $10\ \text{s}$. Find its acceleration.

blocks.title: Doubling the speed
blocks.q: A runner rounds a curve at $4\ \text{m/s}$, then later at $8\ \text{m/s}$ on the same curve. How does the centripetal acceleration change?
steps: $\role[centripetal acceleration]{acceleration}{a_c} = \dfrac{\role[speed]{velocity}{v}^2}{\role[radius]{position}{r}}$: the speed is squared and $r$ is unchanged.

blocks.html: Thinking an object at constant speed can't be accelerating. Acceleration measures any change in velocity, and turning changes the velocity's direction. Check: if the path curves, there is an acceleration with a part toward the inside of the curve.
Try it in the Science Lab: Circles and Gravity: The Apple and the Moon, which compares the Moon's centripetal acceleration with an apple's fall, the comparison Newton made.
